prompt.context: Our client is Rotisserie Ranch, a poultry farming company that specializes in growing chickens for rotisserie roasting. Its primary customer segment is comprised of large grocery chains that buy chickens to fresh roast in the meat departments of their grocery stores. Market research has revealed to Rotisserie Ranch that more and more consumers have begun buying flavored rotisserie chickens recently.
prompt.question: Rotisserie Ranch is thinking of pre-flavoring some of its chickens for grocers. What would you consider in making this recommendation?

clarifying_info.q: What are the industry dynamics around unsold cooked chickens?
clarifying_info.a: Predicting demand for cooked chickens is difficult for grocers; any leftover cooked chickens at the end of the day are thrown out; unthawed chickens cannot be re-frozen.

clarifying_info.q: Does the client have any proprietary capabilities relevant to this product?
clarifying_info.a: The client has a patented process for sterilely packaging chicken so that it will remain fresh for 30 days, making freezing unnecessary. The client is currently the industry market share leader in rotisserie-ready chicken.

clarifying_info.q: What flavors / products are being considered?
clarifying_info.a: Four new flavored products to be introduced concurrently: Barbecue, lemon herb, tandoori, and teriyaki.

clarifying_info.q: Is there competition in the pre-seasoned chicken space?
clarifying_info.a: No competition in the new product market due to the client's patented process.

exhibits.title: Store Sales
exhibits.shows: A table comparing weekly sales, retail price, and retailer margin for two product types (Standard Rotisserie and BBQ Seasoned Rotisserie) across four stores (A, B, C, D).

framework: Assess value to grocery retailers of pre-seasoned chickens (pros and cons)
Determine how to validate demand — design a market test with a control group
Analyze market test results to quantify retailer profit impact
Synthesize findings into a go/no-go recommendation for Rotisserie Ranch

questions.prompt: Do you think grocery retailers would be interested in pre-seasoned chickens from Rotisserie Ranch? Brainstorm reasons they would and would not want this product.
questions.guidance: Strong answers identify both sides. Yes (interested): (1) Labor Cost Reduction — meat department workers no longer need to spend time seasoning chickens; (2) Economies of Scale — centralized seasoning lowers cost; (3) Product Consistency — centrally managed R&D produces more consistent flavor. No (not interested): (1) Loss of Differentiation — grocery chains currently differentiate via value-added in-store preparation; (2) Better Attuned to Local Needs — grocers may better gauge local consumer tastes; (3) Increases Inventory and SKUs — more complexity to manage.

questions.prompt: Grocers are interested but want to be sure the chickens will sell. How would you make sure?
questions.guidance: Candidate should propose a pilot/market test with a control or comparison group before full rollout. Key elements: select representative stores, have control stores selling standard rotisserie chicken, measure sales and profitability over a defined period, then compare results.

questions.prompt: A test market launch for the new Rotisserie Ranch BBQ chicken was administered. Using Exhibit A, calculate the overall profit for both the standard rotisserie stores (A & B) and the BBQ seasoned stores (C & D). What does this tell us?
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply the formula: Retailer profit = Weekly sales × Retailer margin. Then compare total profits across the two product types.

math.setup: Retailer profit = Weekly Sales × Retailer Margin. Compare standard chicken (Stores A & B) vs. BBQ seasoned chicken (Stores C & D).
steps: Difference: $1,075 − $900 = $175 more gross profit per week with BBQ Seasoned
math.answer: Grocers earn $175 more gross profit per week from the BBQ seasoned chicken than from standard rotisserie chicken (assuming test stores are representative).

Economies of Scale: Centralized seasoning lowers unit cost
Product Consistency: Centrally managed process; client can invest more in R&D for flavors

Better Attuned to Local Needs: Grocers may be better at gauging consumer tastes in their specific markets

recommendation: Rotisserie Ranch should launch the pre-seasoned BBQ chicken product and pilot the other three flavors (lemon herb, tandoori, teriyaki).
The market is shifting toward flavored rotisserie chicken and the test results show grocers earn $175 more gross profit per week with the BBQ seasoned product.
risks: Test market stores (C & D) may not be representative of all grocer locations — different demographics or store sizes could affect results.
Margin compression for grocers (25% vs. 30%) could be a concern if volume does not hold up at scale.
Introduction of four flavors simultaneously adds inventory and SKU complexity for both Rotisserie Ranch and its grocery customers.
Grocers who value in-store seasoning as a differentiator may resist the product or negotiate aggressively on price.
next_steps: Roll out BBQ seasoned chicken to a broader set of stores to confirm results are statistically representative.
Run pilot tests for the remaining three flavors (lemon herb, tandoori, teriyaki) before full launch.
Work with grocery partners on shelf placement and marketing to maximize sell-through and minimize end-of-day waste.
Monitor competitive landscape — the patented process provides temporary protection, but Rotisserie Ranch should plan for eventual competition.
